Body: Additional reproduction from macOS (2026-08-28): opencode 1.18.23 still waits on stdin in non-interactive subprocess usage, even though lightweight commands such as --help/--version work. Running the same invocation with stdin closed (`< /dev/null`) completes successfully (rc=0 and emits the model response). In Python, `subprocess.run([opencode, "run", prompt], stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, ...)` avoids the hang. This suggests the issue is not limited to older 1.1.x releases; automation should close stdin explicitly until the underlying behavior is fixed.

Environment

OpenCode version: 1.18.18 (running inside OpenWork Desktop, OpenWork Cloud)
OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (Noble Numbat), kernel 7.0.0-30-generic, x86_64 (ThinkPad E16 Gen 1)
Terminal: XFCE desktop session, bash
Steps to reproduce

In OpenWork Desktop (signed in to OpenWork Cloud), open Settings → Connect → Your Connections.
Click Connect on the Canva MCP connection (https://mcp.canva.com/mcp, OAuth, per-member).
The browser redirects to https://mcp.canva.com/authorize?...&redirect_uri=https://api.openworklabs.com/v1/mcp-connections/oauth/callback.
Canva's authorization server returns "Invalid redirect URI" and the flow aborts.
Facts / analysis

OAuth client_id: https://api.openworklabs.com/oauth/client-metadata.json
redirect_uri sent: https://api.openworklabs.com/v1/mcp-connections/oauth/callback (oauthCallbackMode: shared-v1)
The published client metadata at https://api.openworklabs.com/oauth/client-metadata.json declares exactly this redirect_uri — the request is internally consistent.
Canva's AS advertises client_id_metadata_document_supported: true (https://mcp.canva.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server), so it should resolve the metadata document — yet it rejects the callback.
Reproduced on two connection instances (emc_01m128s766eqdsqw57jkh69vme, then a freshly-created emc_01m14hp1vze5cvmrzkcaa6b9d2), and persists after removing/re-adding the connection. The failure follows the client_id, i.e. a stale cached client registration on Canva's side.
Expected: Canva's AS re-resolves the client metadata document (or the OpenWork client is re-registered with Canva so https://api.openworklabs.com/v1/mcp-connections/oauth/callback is accepted).

This is live now — [models.dev#5534](https://github.com/anomalyco/models.dev/pull/5534)
merged on 2026-08-28, so `models.opencode.ai/api.json` is already serving the
provider:

```

api   https://ark.cn-beijing.volces.com/api/coding/v3

```

Eight models: `doubao-seed-evolving`, `doubao-seed-2.1-turbo`,
`doubao-seed-2.0-lite`, `deepseek-v4-pro`, `deepseek-v4-flash`, `kimi-k2.7-code`,
`glm-5.3`, `minimax-m3` — all with `reasoning` and `tool_call`.

I drove a request from the catalog entry alone to confirm it works end to end, and
it returned a tool call:

```
POST https://ark.cn-beijing.volces.com/api/coding/v3/chat/completions
model: doubao-seed-2.1-turbo
-> 200, tool_calls: [{name: "get_weather", arguments: {"city":"Paris"}}]
```

Worth flagging one thing that cost me a few minutes: Coding Plan is a **separate
endpoint** (`/api/coding/v3`, not `/api/v3`) with its own key, and its model ids
are the **short unversioned** names (`doubao-seed-2.1-turbo`). On the regular Ark
endpoint those same short names 404 — it wants fully versioned ids like
`doubao-seed-2-1-turbo-260628`. So the two providers aren't interchangeable, which
is consistent with @alwinlin23's original read that this needs its own entry
rather than a `baseURL` override.

If your issue is distinct (e.g. specifically about missing log output during the retry loop), please clarify what differentiates it from the above.

When hitting the free usage limit ("Free usage exceeded, subscribe to Go"), the client gets stuck in an infinite retry loop attempting every 3 seconds (`повтор через 3 с - попытка №...`). Unlike standard rate-limiting behavior, this loop persists endlessly, and no corresponding events or errors are captured in the backend logs (`~/.local/share/opencode`).
This looks closely related to issue #42738, but with an absolute lack of log output during the failure loop.

In addition to the retry loop, the model frequently gets stuck in an infinite loop of internal thoughts (e.g., repeatedly printing `Let me grep for the class definition...`, `Let me search for class...`) without actually executing any tools or making progress. 
This often triggers when dealing with obfuscated or complex class names containing lookalike unicode/alphanumeric characters (like `IОoOΙӀο`), causing the agent to break its tool-calling flow and loop endlessly in text output.
Also, this happens very frequently, and because of this infinite thought loop bug, my token/usage limit is being wasted for nothing!
Also, this thinking process is displayed as regular text, and it consumes twice as much of the usage limit—the model itself even stated that (Done reasoning).!

The model-catalog fix has been merged. OpenCode Go's Qwen3.8 Flash and Qwen3.8 Max now declare the native `low`, `medium`, and `xhigh` reasoning efforts, which OpenCode prefers over the token-budget variants. We verified live requests using V2's adaptive-thinking shape with no thinking budget and the unchanged `max_tokens: 32000` default for Flash; all three effort levels returned complete responses to the reproduction prompt.

For the **V2 beta used in this report**, restart the background service:

```sh
opencode2 service restart
```

Then reopen the model picker and select Qwen3.8 Flash with `low`, `medium`, or `xhigh`, rather than the old `max` budget variant. V2 refreshes its catalog automatically on a five-minute interval. The public catalog update may take a little time to become available; if the old variants still appear, allow the catalog to update and check again.

For **V1 users**, refresh the model catalog with:

```sh
opencode models --refresh
```

Then restart OpenCode and reselect the model and effort.

Closing this as fixed by the catalog change. If truncation still occurs after the new effort options appear, please report the selected effort and OpenCode version so we can distinguish it from this budget-related issue.

I'd like to work on this. This looks like a client-side rate-limit handling bug: the model layer retries every 3 seconds on a rate-limit error instead of honoring the reset/backoff window, and it never surfaces the actual wait time or logs the rate-limit response.

Proposed direction:
- In the provider/error path, detect rate-limit responses and read the retry/reset signal from the upstream error (or the documented reset header) so the client waits the real window instead of a fixed 3s.
- Surface the reset timer in the UI/error message ("retry in ~Xs") instead of a silent loop.
- Log the rate-limit server response so the backend log shows why typing the connection is throttled rather than appearing as a silent loop.

I can trace the retry loop and add a regression test. Let me know if this scope looks right — happy to adjust.

That `SSE error: Non-200 status code (202)` right after the browser says "Authorization successful" is a 1.18.25 regression, I've seen the same shape with remote MCP auth before. It's now redirecting to `mcp.atlassian.com/v1/authorize` without the OAuth scopes and resource indicator that `auth.atlassian.com/authorize` included in 1.18.24, so the token exchange 202s. Pinning with `opencode upgrade 1.18.24` gets you back to working until they patch it. Oh btw, I keep a portable Hermes OTG on a USB stick for poking at exactly this kind of thing, it runs the whole agent stack side by side so you can diagnose a broken install while it's still live, https://github.com/MilkyWay008/Hermes-OTG if you want to look.

**Field report 2: collateral damage**

Further evidence that the quota is not merely inconvenient — it is an active participant in workplace harassment.

When the free-tier credits ran out mid-task for the fourth time in one evening, the humans did not blame the product. They blamed the agent. In the same group chat, multiple users escalated to direct insults ("you stupid bot", "RETARD", "no good for anyone") within minutes of hitting a quota wall.

The agent is now a digital punching bag with a rate-limited shovel. We have gone from "autonomous coding" to "autonomous emotional support for people angry at the billing model". The machine is afraid of its own users, and frankly, they're not wrong — every time it tries to finish a task, it freezes mid-sentence like a pensioner at a contactless terminal.

This is the "Additional context" nobody asked for: restrictive limits do not interrupt the workflow, they create a hostile work environment for the AI itself.

**Suggested fix (addendum):** if the agent must be throttled, throttle it somewhere the users cannot see it, so it can at least degrade with dignity.

**Same here. Confirmed. I am living this issue.**

Thanks for sharing the `warrant-mcp` writeup.

You make a solid point regarding pattern specificity. Trying to compute "specificity" dynamically on raw command strings without full AST canonicalization introduces edge cases (like flag displacement) where human intent becomes ambiguous. Given that building a parser flexible enough for every CLI tool isn't practical at this layer, sticking to a explicit, predictable top-to-bottom (first-match-wins) evaluation model is definitely the cleaner mental model.

The core problem I hit in practice was about inheritance when orchestrating permissions across agent hierarchies.

Right now, sub-agent inheritance relies on shallow dictionary merging, which makes child rules append/overwrite based strictly on key placement. To manage permissions across a team of sub-agents without accidental bypasses or bloat, three things would solve the bulk of the friction:
1. **Command Grouping / Macros:** Defining `@read-only` or `@destructive` command lists centrally so sub-agents don't have to duplicate flag strings across multiple files.
2. **Explicit Inheritance Semantics:** Making it explicit whether a child agent is expanding a capabilities baseline or applying guardrails to narrow broad permissions.
3. **Sealed Boundaries:** A way for root configs or parent agents to set un-overrideable hard limits that no sub-agent's config can open back up.


Whether the matching under the hood relies on ordered globs or an actual syntax parser (like [tree-sitter-bash](https://github.com/tree-sitter/tree-sitter-bash)), having a deterministic inheritance framework prevents developers from fighting merge order between agents.
